title: th says /th/ (voiced)
parentNote: Today's sound is the buzzy th at the start of "this" and "that" — the one where the tongue actually comes out between the teeth and hums. Nearly every child hides the tongue and swaps in a /d/, so "this" becomes "dis" and "that" becomes "dat"; it is the single most predictable error in the whole of English phonics and it is nothing to worry about. The fix is to make it visible and feelable: put your tongue out where they can see it, then have them press a finger on their throat and feel the buzz that /d/ does not have. There is a quieter th as well, the one in "thin", and that gets a day of its own much later — today is only the buzzy one.

activities.mouthCue: Tongue tip pokes out between your teeth and hums. You should be able to see it and feel it buzz.
activities.prompt: This one you can hold on for as long as you have breath. Watch my tongue come out.
These two get muddled all the time. One keeps the tongue hidden. Find the one where it pokes out.
Three pairs of letters, three different sounds. Only one of them buzzes.
Three sounds. Start with the tongue out and buzzing, and finish with a quiet hiss.
This means the one over there. Same buzzy start, different middle.
Now th is at the end instead. Round your lips first, then out comes the tongue.
This is a comparing word — bigger than, faster than. It turns up a lot once we can write those.
Both end the same way. Is there a buzz at the front or not?
Same start, same middle. Does the end buzz or does it hiss?
One of these keeps the tongue behind the teeth. Listen to the first sound only.
